analysis.one_liner: Shields federal farm marketing orders from antitrust lawsuits.
analysis.headline: The bill attracted no cosponsors and died in House committees, never reaching a floor vote before the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal marketing orders let growers of a crop — like raisins, almonds, or milk — act together to limit how much reaches the market, which supports higher prices. Normally antitrust laws forbid that kind of coordination, but farm marketing orders already enjoy broad legal protection. This bill would have gone further, writing into law that no action taken under a marketing order could ever be challenged under antitrust law. A court case had found some marketing-order conduct vulnerable, so producers wanted an airtight shield. The bill was referred to the Judiciary and Agriculture Committees, sent to subcommittees, and died there with no cosponsors and no vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Producers of commodities covered by federal marketing orders — dairy farmers, citrus growers, raisin and almond producers — would have gained certainty that their government-sanctioned coordination on volumes, quality, and prices could never be challenged as an antitrust violation. No consumer group or ordinary household stood to benefit; the effect on the public runs the other way, through prices.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Commodity producers under federal marketing orders

how_it_helps.text: The bill added a new subsection to the Agricultural Adjustment Act declaring that no action, regulation, decision, determination, or other act or omission of anyone acting for the Secretary of Agriculture with respect to an agricultural marketing order could be construed to violate the antitrust laws.

Its sponsor was a California Democrat, Calvin Dooley, whose district included producers of specialty crops like raisins, tree fruit, and cotton that are heavily governed by federal marketing orders; the exemption would have protected those supply-management programs from lawsuits.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers would bear the cost. Marketing orders work by restricting supply or disciplining how a commodity is sold, which supports prices above what an open market would produce; immunizing every action under those orders from antitrust challenge would lock in higher prices at the grocery store with no offsetting benefit to shoppers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Shoppers paying prices supported by supply controls

drawbacks.text: The bill would have made it harder to challenge coordinated actions that raise food prices. Marketing orders let producers of a commodity jointly restrict what reaches the market; shielding those actions completely from antitrust review means consumers have no legal recourse if the coordination pushes prices up.

The exemption swept extremely broadly: it covered 'any act or omission' of anyone acting under the Secretary of Agriculture's authority on a marketing order, which could have shielded conduct far beyond routine administration.

A good-faith supporter would acknowledge the bill was unnecessary for ordinary legislation: marketing orders are issued under a 1937 law that already gives them substantial antitrust protection, and the bill was mainly a belt-and-suspenders response to court rulings that had found some marketing-order actions vulnerable to antitrust challenge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit would have gone to a narrow set of producers: legal certainty that federal marketing orders could coordinate prices and supplies without antitrust risk. The cost would have been spread thinly across every household that buys dairy, fruit, nuts, and vegetables, in the form of prices sustained by government-backed coordination. Federal marketing orders already carry significant antitrust immunity, so the bill's practical gain was modest for producers, but what gain it offered would have come directly at consumers' expense. On balance, the bill served a concentrated producer interest, and its quiet death left consumers no worse off.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Judiciary and Agriculture Committees and their subcommittees, got an request for the Agriculture Department's comments, and then sat with no further action until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Calvin Dooley of California introduced the bill on October 24, 1997; it was referred to both the Judiciary and Agriculture Committees.
A week later, it was assigned to the Risk Management and Specialty Crops subcommittee on the Agriculture side and the Livestock, Dairy and Poultry subcommittee.
On November 13, 1997, the House requested an executive comment from the USDA — a routine step asking the executive branch's opinion — and that was the last action recorded.
No other member signed on as a cosponsor, and no committee marked up the bill or sent it to the floor before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Food consumers and anyone who might have challenged marketing-order coordination in court are better off, since the antitrust shield was never enacted. Producers who wanted guaranteed immunity lost nothing of substance, since existing law already gives marketing orders strong protection.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Food consumers; the antitrust shield never became law

for.name: Rep. Calvin M. Dooley (D-CA)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to exempt marketing-order actions from the antitrust laws; it was referred to two committees.

against.name: House Judiciary and Agriculture Committees
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral, sent it to subcommittees, requested USDA comments, and never scheduled a markup or reported it out — the bill never reached the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never drew a floor vote or a committee vote, so no partisan split was ever recorded; it had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party.

industries.industry: Specialty crop producers under federal marketing orders (dairy, citrus, almonds, raisins, and other commodities)
industries.note: The bill would have guaranteed that marketing-order actions—coordinated production limits, quality rules, and marketing controls—could never be challenged under antitrust law. That locks in the ability of producers in these commodities to act collectively to limit supply and support prices.

Consumers pay the prices that marketing orders are designed to support. Broadening the antitrust shield for these producer programs would tend to keep food prices higher than a competitive market would set.

industries.industry: Agricultural handlers and processors (buyers of regulated commodities)
industries.note: Handlers who buy from producers must administer marketing-order deductions and volume controls. A fuller antitrust exemption clarifies the rules they operate under, but also entrenches the producer programs they must comply with.
